beats.care: Start a side hustle or sell online? A GST slip-up is now far less likely to become a police case.
beats.what: The GST Council took away GST officers' power to arrest people, and raised the bar for criminal cases to ₹5 crore.
beats.why: Businesses complained of harassment. The idea: trust taxpayers and save tough action for big frauds.

cards.body: On 8 Oct, the GST Council (the Finance Minister plus state ministers who run GST) met for the 57th time. It decided to remove GST officers' power to arrest people, and raised the limit for criminal prosecution from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore of tax.
Up from ₹1 crore. Smaller cases get handled with penalties instead.
cards.caption: new minimum tax amount for a criminal case

cards.body: GST is the tax added to almost everything you buy, from Maggi to phones. Businesses collect it and pay it to the government. If a business cheats, officers investigate. Until now, they could even arrest people in serious cases.
cards.title: wait, what's GST again?

cards.body: If you run a small business, freelance or sell online, a GST mistake is now less likely to turn into a police matter. Cheating on tax is still punishable, just with a higher bar before it becomes a criminal case.
cards.title: if you ever start a side hustle

cards.body: Not every state was happy: five states opposed taking away the arrest powers, raising concerns about how GST rules will be enforced.

a.body: Honest businesses feared harassment. Trust them, and save tough action for big frauds.
a.label: Supporters say

b.body: Without arrest powers, it may be harder to stop large tax cheating.
b.label: States that opposed it worry

opts: The GST Council: the Centre plus the states
cards.why: The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, includes state finance ministers.

cards.q: Removing GST arrest powers: good move?

hook: GST officers *can't arrest you* anymore. Wait, they could before?
